metadata.description_blurb: Two teams, one pipeline, identical output. One supervised it; one didn't. This teardown unpacks what genuine AI oversight actually requires — testable handoffs, reversibility gates, an 8-item accountability map, and the Boondoggle Score no one validated. Nine minutes on the accountability gap at the center of AI deployment.
chapters: Act I: Identical Code, One Difference
Act III: Not a Feeling — A Line in the Audit Trail
Act VI: The Data Is in the Log
metadata.source_chapter: Computational Skepticism for AI — Ch. 9: Delegation and Trust

beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's the whole chapter in one experiment. Two teams build the same loan-scoring pipeline — same data, same model, same fairness metrics. Diff the code, you can't tell them apart. Both ship. Then the committee asks each team one question: who is responsible if a decision is challenged? One team answers in writing. The other goes quiet. Nothing in the code differed. One thing did. So what was the single variable that decided the rollout?

props.command: Two teams, one identical pipeline, one difference — who's accountable when a loan decision is challenged?
props.runningText: delegation — a contract, not a partition of labor…
output: The code was identical — the documentation was not
One team could name what each human verified; the other couldn't
The only variable was the delegation map

beats.narration_text: Act one. A controlled experiment that ran itself — two teams, one pipeline, one difference.

lines: The Two Teams

beats.narration_text: Same data. Same model. Same fairness metrics. Same monitoring. On paper, the same system. The only difference lived in the documentation — one sentence versus a page. That page is the whole story.

left.label: TEAM 1 — 'the loan officer reviews and decides'

right.label: TEAM 2 — verify the explanation, run the checklist, record one of four codes

beats.narration_text: The committee asks one question: who is responsible? Follow team one's pipeline. The AI produced the score. The officer reviews. But review means what — checked how, against what criteria? The accountability arrow runs to a word nobody defined, and dead-ends. Team two's arrow lands on a named human.

manim.spec: two identical pipelines side by side; an 'accountability' arrow traced through each; team 1's arrow reaches an undefined 'reviews' node and dead-ends in terracotta; team 2's arrow lands on a named human node

lines: One arrow lands on a person. One dead-ends at a word.

beats.narration_text: Picture the room. The committee waits. The team that can't answer isn't incompetent — their pipeline runs, loans get scored, decisions get made. They simply cannot say, in writing, what their own system does. So the rollout is tabled. Not for a bad model. For a missing sentence.

props.title: The Committee Question

left.label: TEAM 1 — pipeline runs fine
left.note: loans scored , model accurate , metrics green

right.label: ROLLOUT TABLED — cannot answer in writing
right.note: not for a bad model — for a missing sentence

props.sparkLine: Not for a bad model. For a missing sentence.

beats.narration_text: Act two. The load-bearing idea — and everything else hangs off it.

lines: Contract, Not Partition

props.command: render a Manim scene: an untestable handoff — 'the AI produces a reasonable result and the human reviews it' — fans into five different officer behaviors; a testable one — score 0–1, accept / re-score / override, four justification codes — collapses to one auditable log row

beats.narration_text: The mistake almost everyone makes is to treat delegation as a partition — the AI does this slice, I do that slice, like cutting a pie. A partition only names who touches what. A contract has boundaries, obligations, and a clause for when a party fails to deliver. Delegation is the contract.

props.title: Partition vs Contract

left.label: PARTITION — who touches what
left.note: slices the pie; no obligations, no failure clause

right.label: CONTRACT — boundaries, obligations, a failure clause
right.note: and what happens when the handoff fails

props.sparkLine: A pie slice carries no obligations.

beats.narration_text: Here's the test. The AI produces a reasonable result, the human reviews it. Hand that to five officers and you get five behaviors, all called reviewing — no fact of the matter about whether it worked. Now: score zero to one; accept, re-score, or override with one of four codes. A stranger reads the log and knows exactly what happened.

manim.spec: top: the phrase 'reasonable result / human reviews' fans out into five divergent officer-behavior branches; bottom: 'score 0–1, accept/re-score/override, one of four codes' collapses into a single auditable log row; terracotta on the one readable row

lines: Five behaviors → one auditable row

beats.narration_text: This is the unglamorous part, and the unglamour is the point. Write the condition. Circle every interpretive word — reasonable, review, appropriate. Replace each with a criterion a stranger could check. Nobody gets promoted for this. It's the entire difference between a supervised pipeline and one that only looks supervised.

manim.spec: two-column: interpretive words (reviews/reasonable/appropriate) with terracotta ring on left; arrows to testable criteria on right; spark: nobody gets promoted for this

lines: Circle every interpretive word. Replace it.

beats.narration_text: One honest wrinkle. Some conditions are testable only by a qualified reviewer — verify the citation is accurate in the domain-specific sense. That's real, but narrower than anyone-can-check. The line isn't a clean binary; it's graded. The standard still holds — honest documentation just says which tier a handoff sits in.

lines: Not a binary — a tier.
Tier A — any non-author can verify on a sample case
Tier B — only a qualified reviewer can (domain judgment)

beats.act: ACT III — Five Capacities, Five Artifacts
beats.narration_text: Act three. Five supervisory capacities — and here's the reframe that stings: none is a trait you have. Each is an operational form the pipeline either contains or does not. Plausibility auditing is a checklist. Problem formulation is a written spec. If the artifact is missing, the capacity did not happen.

lines: A capacity is a job, not a virtue.
Plausibility auditing — a verification checklist, answered yes/no
Problem formulation — a written scoping spec

beats.act: judgment is a line, not a feeling
beats.narration_text: Engineers hear supervisory capacity and reach for words like judgment and experience — words that describe a person, not a task. But watch what's actually happening. Interpretive judgment isn't a feeling in the reviewer's chest. It's a line in the audit trail: the decision was X because the score was Y, in this context, meaning Z.

lines: Not a feeling — a line in the log.
decision:       DECLINED
score:          0.23  ,  threshold: 0.35

beats.narration_text: So the map carries eight items per step. Name, owner, inputs, outputs — items one through four, standard engineering. Then handoff condition, failure mode, verification, audit trail — items five through eight. The first four any competent team writes. The last four are the supervisory additions almost everyone omits.

lines: 1–4 are engineering. 5–8 are supervision.
1 Step name & purpose , 2 Owner , 3 Inputs
5 Handoff condition — testable (the load-bearing clause)

beats.narration_text: And here's the trap. A pipeline missing items one to four is broken — it won't run, so the gap announces itself. A pipeline missing five to eight is unsupervised — and it runs beautifully. The failure that costs you is the one that never stops the pipeline. It surfaces downstream, usually found by the person it harmed.

manim.spec: two pipelines; the 'broken' one halts loudly at a red gap (items 1–4 missing); the 'unsupervised' one flows smoothly while an undetected error propagates downstream toward a harmed user; a rising attrition curve tracks the silent error; terracotta on the downstream harm

lines: Broken announces itself. Unsupervised runs beautifully.

beats.narration_text: Act four. Before the map — which sub-tasks should the AI touch at all? Five questions.

lines: The Boondoggle Questions

beats.narration_text: Five questions, asked of every sub-task. Verification cost — can a human check it cheaply, or does checking cost as much as doing it. Stakes — the price of being wrong. Distribution match — in-distribution, or a tail case. Reversibility — can the action be undone. Audit trail — does it leave a reviewable trace.

Reversibility is the sharpest one. A reversible action — a draft you can discard — tolerates a high error rate. An irreversible one — a delete, a send, a wire transfer — should sit behind an explicit human-approval gate, almost without exception. Not a vote the AI can win. A gate a human has to open.

manim.spec: reversible actions (a draft) flow through freely; irreversible actions labeled delete / send / wire arrive at a closed gate that only a human hand opens; contrast a 'vote' (AI can win) against a 'gate' (human must open); terracotta on the gate

lines: Irreversible → a gate a human has to open

beats.narration_text: And verification cost isn't a character test — it's economics acting on attention. When checking an output costs as much as producing it, the cost structure itself quietly pushes the supervisor toward accepting rather than checking. Expensive-to-verify tasks are dangerous precisely because the pressure to wave them through is structural.

manim.spec: x-axis: verification cost; y-axis: pressure to accept without checking; rising terracotta curve; green cheaply-verifiable zone left; danger zone right; spark: the pressure is structural

lines: Cost structure pushes attention toward 'accept'

beats.narration_text: The five answers sort each sub-task into three buckets — appropriate for the AI, human-only, or hybrid with verification at a named handoff. But the output isn't the bucket. It's the written justification for the choice. And a caveat I owe you: this score is one engineer's heuristic, not a validated instrument. The questions matter more than any number.

manim.spec: sub-task tokens fall through the five questions and sort into three labeled bins — AI / human-only / hybrid; the emitted artifact is a 'documented justification' card, not a verdict stamp; terracotta on 'documented justification'

lines: Not a verdict — a documented justification

beats.narration_text: Act five. Enough abstraction. Watch the map fall out of one real pipeline.

lines: The Paper Summarizer

beats.narration_text: A research-paper summarizer with citation verification. Six steps. The AI owns parsing, extraction, formatting — the pattern work. A human owns the taxonomy, the plausibility audit, and the final sign-off — the judgment work. Three of six steps are irreducibly human. And notice: the human steps are the ones that look like review, not work.

lines: AI does the pattern work. The human does the judgment work.
Step 1 , HUMAN — define the section taxonomy
Step 2 , AI — parse into sections (nothing dropped)

beats.narration_text: The two highest-risk handoffs are both AI-to-human. Step three into four: the danger is the researcher waves through a high-confidence extraction and a domain-critical qualification vanishes. Step five into six: treating a sign-off as proofreading instead of interpretation — and a misleading framing ships.

manim.spec: the six-step chain drawn left to right; the two AI→human seams (3→4 and 5→6) glow terracotta; at seam 3→4 a qualifier token 'on the training set only' drops out of the stream unless a human catch icon intercepts it

lines: Both riskiest handoffs are AI → human

beats.narration_text: Watch it happen at reading speed. Step three hands up a clean, confident summary. The claim reads: this method outperformed the baselines. Fluent. Specific. It looks exactly right — which is the whole problem.

lines: Clean. Confident. Complete.
Method:      transformer-based scoring pipeline
Performance: outperformed the baselines  ✓ high confidence

beats.narration_text: Now open the source. The paper didn't say outperformed the baselines. It said outperformed them on the training set only. Five words the model dropped — and with them, the entire meaning of the result. The proxy read fluent. The truth had a qualifier.

right.label: SOURCE — 'outperformed on the training set only'
right.note: five words that change the meaning of the result

beats.narration_text: Step four is the human catch. Open the PDF, verify no qualification was dropped, spot-check one in five high-confidence entries, then sign. That is not proofreading. It is the step where the pipeline earns the word supervised — or quietly loses it.

lines: This is not proofreading.
✓  Open source PDF — compare each claim to source text
✓  No qualification dropped — 'on the training set only' RESTORED

beats.act: looks good is not a handoff condition
beats.narration_text: Notice what the score never contains: reasonable, human reviews, check for accuracy. Every human action names what's checked, against what, at what granularity. Looks good is not a handoff condition — tattoo that somewhere. And the score flags one gap: no step does executive integration. Fine for one user. The moment a second person relies on the output, a step is missing.

lines: Specificity is the whole difference.
Banned words: 'reasonable', 'human reviews', 'check for accuracy'
Every human step names what , against what , at what granularity

beats.act: ACT VI — Trust You Can Watch
beats.narration_text: Act six. There is a property you can monitor in deployment, and most deployments don't. Calibrated trust: the supervisor's reliance should match the AI's actual reliability on this kind of case. Too little reliance is undertrust — you lose the value. Too much is overtrust — you accept what you shouldn't. Only the middle is calibration.

manim.spec: a horizontal axis undertrust → calibrated → overtrust; a 'reliance' curve overlaid on an 'actual reliability' curve; the region where they match is lit terracotta; the two mismatch zones labeled undertrust (lose value) and overtrust (accept errors)

lines: Trust You Can Watch

beats.narration_text: Overtrust is the quiet one. It's automation complacency — monitoring degrades under a low rate of signals — documented at length in the human-automation literature. It produces no immediate flags. Just uncaught errors, surfacing later, often found by the affected user. Whether it's the most common failure in AI today, I hold as a working hypothesis, not a finding.

props.title: Overtrust — The Invisible Failure
props.note: vigilance decays under low signal rates; errors surface downstream, not on

props.segment: Reading calibration off the audit trail
props.command: render a Manim scene: 200 cases — 186 accepted, 14 overridden; a 40-case ground-truth sample finds 6 AI errors; compute override rate ≈ 7% vs estimated error rate ≈ 15%; drop the point on the undertrust — calibrated — overtrust axis

beats.narration_text: Here's calibration as arithmetic — an illustrative case. Two hundred decisions: the human overrode fourteen, a seven percent override rate. But a forty-case audit finds six real errors — about fifteen percent. The human is overriding half as often as the AI is wrong. That gap is overtrust, and it's sitting right there in the audit trail.

manim.spec: write-on two fractions: override rate 14/200 ≈ 7% and estimated error rate 6/40 ≈ 15%; a point lands in the 'overtrust' zone of the calibration axis; terracotta on the gap between the two rates; label numbers as an illustrative worked case

lines: Override 7% vs error 15% — that gap is overtrust

beats.narration_text: And this is the field's most closable failure. The disposition data — confirmed, corrected, unverifiable — is already in the log. Nobody has to build anything. Someone just has to look. The gap isn't between having the data and collecting it. It's between having it and reading it.

lines: The data is in the log. Someone has to look.
confirmed  (accepted):    139 decisions , 69.5%
corrected  (override):     14 decisions ,  7.0%

beats.narration_text: Which is what the AI Use Disclosure is for — a supervisory log, if it's four things: granular per step, honest about corrections, time-stamped, tied to evidence. When the disclosure records that step three dropped a qualifier and a human caught it — that's not embarrassing. That's the data proving the pipeline works.

lines: A correction is not embarrassing — it's proof of work.
Granular — one entry per step
Honest — records corrections and gaps, not just clean handoffs

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The verdict on delegation. A delegation is not a partition of labor — it's a contract, and its load-bearing clause is the handoff condition, which has exactly one property: it has to be testable, even if only by a qualified reviewer. The five supervisory capacities aren't traits — they're jobs with artifacts, and if the artifact is missing, the capacity didn't happen. The map's last four items separate a supervised pipeline from one that merely looks supervised — because the failure that costs you is the one that never stops the pipeline. And trust calibration is a property you can watch in the audit trail — the field's most closable gap is simply reading the data you already have.

artifactLines: Delegation is a contract, not a partition — boundaries, obligations, a failure clause.
The handoff condition is the load-bearing clause — and it must be testable.
A capacity with no artifact did not happen.
Map items 5–8 separate supervised from unsupervised — the silent failure is the costly one.
Trust calibration is monitorable — reliance should match reliability, per case.
'Looks good' is not a handoff condition.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: Take one AI pipeline you actually run. First, before you fix anything, reconstruct its delegation map as it is — for each step, the owner, the inputs, the outputs, and be honest about whether the handoff is vague or testable. Then rewrite it: give every step a handoff condition a stranger could check on a sample case, and name what happens when it fails. End quote. That's the chapter, compressed. The point isn't the tidy final map. It's the reconstruction — because writing down what your pipeline actually does, as opposed to what you remember it doing, is usually where you find the step nobody was supervising. Run it on something you rely on.

props.topic: YOUR TURN — IT RUNS BEAUTIFULLY. NOBODY'S WATCHING.
props.command: Take one AI pipeline you actually run. First reconstruct its delegation map as-is — per step: owner, inputs, outputs, and honestly whether each handoff is vague or testable. Then rewrite it so every handoff condition is checkable by a non-author on a sample case, and name what happens when it fails.
props.runningText: reconstruct as-is — then rewrite every handoff testable — then find the step nobody supervised…

beats.narration_text: It Runs Beautifully. Nobody's Watching. Delegation and trust, from Computational Skepticism for AI. Liam, in for Bear.
